lessons.title: Air, combustion and rusting
lessons.programRef: Form 3 Chemistry — Air, combustion, rusting, water and solubility (to be checked)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: State the composition of air and describe how nitrogen and oxygen are obtained from liquid air.
Describe combustion, tests for oxygen and carbon dioxide and the preparation of oxygen.
Describe the conditions for rusting and methods of rust prevention; name major air pollutants.
reviewNotes: Boiling points of N₂ (−196 °C), Ar (−186 °C) and O₂ (−183 °C) are standard; percentage composition rounded. Safety: burning magnesium and any use of gas cylinders are teacher demonstrations.

blocks.title: Composition and separation of air
blocks.md: Dry air: about **78 % nitrogen, 21 % oxygen**, about 0.9 % argon, about 0.04 % carbon dioxide and traces of other gases. The gases are separated by **fractional distillation of liquid air**: air is cooled until liquid, then warmed, and the gases boil off at different temperatures (nitrogen at −196 °C, argon at −186 °C, oxygen at −183 °C). Uses: nitrogen in making ammonia and fertilisers, oxygen in medicine and welding, argon in light bulbs.

blocks.title: Combustion and tests
blocks.md: **Combustion** is burning in oxygen, giving heat and light. Metals form **oxides**: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO. Non-metals form **acidic oxides**: C + O₂ → CO₂ and S + O₂ → SO₂; methane: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O. Oxygen can be made in the laboratory by decomposing hydrogen peroxide with manganese(IV) oxide as a **catalyst**: 2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂. Tests: **oxygen relights a glowing splint**; **carbon dioxide turns limewater milky**.

blocks.caption: Rusting needs both air (oxygen) and water.
blocks.alt: Three test tubes with an iron nail: dry air gives no rust; boiled water under oil gives no rust; air and water gives rust.

blocks.title: Rusting
blocks.md: **Rusting** is the slow reaction of iron with **oxygen and water**: iron + oxygen + water → hydrated iron(III) oxide (rust). Salt speeds it up (coastal towns like Limbe and Douala). Prevention: **painting, oiling, plastic coating, galvanising** (zinc coating), **sacrificial protection** with a more reactive metal, and using **stainless steel** (an alloy).

blocks.title: Air pollution
blocks.md: **Carbon monoxide** (from incomplete burning of fuel, charcoal or wood) is **poisonous**: never run an engine or burn charcoal in a closed room. **Sulphur dioxide** and **oxides of nitrogen** cause **acid rain**. **Carbon dioxide** and methane are **greenhouse gases**. Smoke particles harm the lungs. Reduce pollution with cleaner fuels, ventilation, catalytic converters and tree planting.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Rusting needs **both** oxygen and water: either alone is not enough.
- A catalyst is not used up: manganese(IV) oxide is unchanged at the end of the reaction.
- Carbon monoxide has no smell; you cannot rely on smell to warn you.

blocks.title: Percentage of oxygen
blocks.statement: In an experiment 60 cm³ of air is passed over heated copper until the volume stops changing at 47.4 cm³. Find the percentage of oxygen.

blocks.title: Rust prevention
blocks.statement: Explain why galvanised (zinc-coated) iron roofing sheets last longer.
steps: The zinc coating keeps oxygen and water away from the iron.
If scratched, zinc, being more reactive, corrodes first and protects the iron.
blocks.answer: Zinc coats and protects the iron.

lessons.title: Water, solubility and hard water
lessons.programRef: Form 3 Chemistry — Air, combustion, rusting, water and solubility (to be checked)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Describe the solvent properties of water and read a solubility curve.
Distinguish temporary and permanent hardness and describe how hardness is removed.
Describe the main steps in water treatment and sources of water pollution.
reviewNotes: Solubility values for KNO₃ (13, 32, 64, 110, 169, 246 g per 100 g at 0, 20, 40, 60, 80, 100 °C) are approximate textbook values; check against the data booklet used in school.
Water treatment and safe-water advice are general and to be reviewed by a public-health worker.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Water as a solvent
blocks.md: Water dissolves many ionic compounds and some covalent ones, so natural water always contains dissolved substances. The **solubility** of a solid is the mass that dissolves in **100 g of water** at a given temperature to make a **saturated solution**. For most solids solubility **increases with temperature**; gases become **less** soluble when hot. Cooling a hot saturated solution makes the extra solute **crystallise**.

blocks.caption: Solubility curve of potassium nitrate in water (approximate values).
blocks.alt: A graph of solubility in grams per 100 grams of water against temperature, rising from about 13 at 0 degrees to 32 at 20, 64 at 40, 110 at 60, 169 at 80 and 246 at 100 degrees.

blocks.title: Hard and soft water
blocks.md: **Hard water** contains dissolved **calcium and magnesium ions**, from rocks such as limestone; it does not easily make a lather with soap and forms **scum**. **Temporary hardness** (calcium hydrogencarbonate) is removed by **boiling**: Ca(HCO₃)₂ → CaCO₃ + H₂O + CO₂; the solid forms **scale** in kettles and pipes. **Permanent hardness** (calcium sulphate) is not removed by boiling but by **washing soda** (sodium carbonate) or an **ion-exchange** resin: Na₂CO₃ + CaSO₄ → CaCO₃ + Na₂SO₄.

blocks.title: Water treatment and pollution
blocks.md: Town supply: **screening**, **coagulation and settling**, **filtration** through sand, and **chlorination** to kill germs. Distilled water is the purest and is used in laboratories. Water is **polluted** by sewage, fertiliser run-off, oil, chemicals from mines and factories and plastic waste. Do not drink water of unknown quality: **boil it** or treat it first.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Solubility is quoted **per 100 g of water**, not per litre of solution.
- Boiling removes only **temporary** hardness.
- Soft water is not necessarily purer or safer; it simply lathers well.

blocks.title: Mass that crystallises
blocks.statement: A saturated solution of potassium nitrate containing 100 g of water at 60 °C is cooled to 20 °C. Use the graph values (110 g and 32 g per 100 g) to find the mass of crystals.
steps: At 60 °C: 110 g dissolved. At 20 °C: only 32 g can stay dissolved.

blocks.title: Which type of hardness?
blocks.statement: A kettle forms scale, and the water also lathers badly again after boiling. Explain.
steps: Scale (CaCO₃) comes from temporary hardness removed by boiling.
If hardness remains after boiling, part of it is permanent hardness.
blocks.answer: Both temporary and permanent hardness are present.
